claims.text: Established physical and chemical fabrication methods can produce near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles.
Significant atomic-size mismatch among constituent elements produces greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion makes nanoparticles more likely to preserve structural and chemical integrity under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
Composition can be varied to create high- and low-atomic-size-mismatch groups while maintaining near-equiatomic ratios.
The relevant catalytic service-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric service-temperature range is 473–1923 K.
Lattice distortion increases the activation barrier for atomic diffusion.
Higher diffusion barriers retard phase separation.
Higher diffusion barriers retard nanoparticle coarsening.
Greater lattice distortion creates a more rugged energy landscape for atomic rearrangement.
The rugged energy landscape inhibits phase segregation and grain growth at high temperature.
Inhibiting atomic rearrangement helps maintain a homogeneous solid-solution structure and chemical stability.
High-distortion nanoparticles will exhibit less phase separation than low-distortion nanoparticles under the same thermal conditions.
High-distortion nanoparticles will exhibit less grain growth than low-distortion nanoparticles under the same thermal conditions.
High-distortion nanoparticles will retain greater compositional uniformity than low-distortion nanoparticles under the same thermal conditions.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply when atomic-size differences are the dominant source of lattice distortion.
Specific electronic interactions or chemical ordering may diminish or eliminate the stabilizing effect attributed to lattice distortion.
The relative contributions of lattice distortion, electronic structure, and chemical affinity may vary among element combinations.
A lack of statistically significant stability improvement in the high-distortion group, or greater degradation in that group, would falsify the hypothesis.
